planting.note: Plant a container-grown rosette or a rooted offset in spring into a lean, mineral, fast-draining mix in full sun; this Brazilian lithophyte grows in bare rock crevices in the wild and resents any soil that stays damp, so treat it more like a rock-garden cactus than a typical bromeliad.

directions: Grow in a lean, gritty, mineral mix with sharp drainage in full sun; Dyckia marnier-lapostollei forms a solitary, stemless rosette of stiff, triangular, silvery-white leaves so densely coated in reflective trichomes that the whole plant reads as nearly pure white, a trait that gave rise to its trade name 'Naked Lady' among specialist growers. It is slower and more solitary than the clumping D. brevifolia, rarely producing more than an occasional pup, so most propagation is by seed or by removing the few offsets that do form. In summer, mature plants send up a modest flower spike with tubular orange-yellow blooms above the foliage, though the silvery rosette itself is the main ornamental draw. It is less cold-hardy than the common clumping dyckias and appreciates winter protection or container culture outside the mildest xeriscape climates.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into lean, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun; Turquoise Puya is a robust Chilean mountain bromeliad, close kin to Puya alpestris, that needs several years of vegetative growth before it is large enough to bloom.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun, giving it plenty of room since mature clumps become large and heavily armed. Puya berteroniana forms a coarse rosette of stiff, silvery, hook-spined leaves and, once established, sends up a stout flower spike several feet tall packed with an extraordinary metallic teal-green flower color set off by vivid orange anthers, one of the most striking color combinations in the plant kingdom. Native to the coastal ranges and foothills of central Chile, it tolerates drought, poor soil, and brief light frost once mature, but resists blooming for years while it builds up rosette size. Because the spiny foliage can snag skin and clothing, site it away from paths and give it several feet of clearance on all sides.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil, well away from foot traffic; Puya chilensis eventually forms a massive, densely spined rosette and needs years of growth before it reaches flowering size.

directions: Site in full sun in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil, giving the plant a wide berth from paths and seating areas. Puya chilensis is a huge Chilean terrestrial bromeliad forming a broad rosette of long, gray-green, wickedly hook-spined leaves so effective at snaring wandering livestock that it earned the nickname 'sheep-eating plant' in its native habitat. After a decade or more of vegetative growth, it produces a massive branched flower spike up to ten feet tall bearing hundreds of dull yellow-green blooms that draw nectar-feeding birds. It tolerates drought, heat, and poor rocky soil with ease and takes brief light frost once established, but it is a plant for large open xeriscape beds rather than tight garden spaces given its eventual size and formidable armament.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; Chagualillo is a smaller, more compact Puya from the coastal hills of central Chile that reaches flowering size faster than the giant Puya species and suits smaller xeriscape beds.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil. Puya venusta is a smaller, tidier terrestrial bromeliad than its giant Chilean relatives, forming a modest rosette of narrow, silvery, spine-edged leaves that stays in scale with typical garden beds. In late winter through spring it sends up a slender flower spike carrying an unusual blue-to-violet flower color that stands out sharply against the silvery foliage. In the wild it is a rare coastal endemic found on only a few Chilean hillsides, so garden cultivation also serves as a useful ex-situ population; give it excellent drainage and avoid summer irrigation once established, since it is adapted to a dry-summer, wet-winter Mediterranean rainfall pattern.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or transplants in spring into rocky, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; this Trans-Pecos Texas native bromeliad handles the hard freezes and bone-dry summers of the Chihuahuan Desert with ease once established.

directions: Plant in rocky, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; Hechtia texensis is a true Texas native, found wild on limestone terraces and gravel flats of the Big Bend region, and is easily mistaken at a glance for a small Agave lechuguilla until its rosette flushes deep red along the leaf margins and tips in strong sun. Unlike agaves it is dioecious, with separate male and female plants, and mature clumps send up a branched flowering stalk with small, brownish-white flowers in spring. It is one of the most cold-hardy terrestrial bromeliads available, taking the genuine hard freezes of the Trans-Pecos high desert, which makes it a genuinely useful architectural accent for Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country xeriscape and rock gardens where more tender bromeliads fail. Established clumps slowly multiply by basal offsets that can be divided to start new colonies.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or transplants in spring into gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun; Guapilla is a spreading Mexican terrestrial bromeliad that colonizes limestone outcrops and dry hillsides from the Chihuahuan Desert to the Gulf coastal plain of northeastern Mexico and southern Texas.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; Guapilla forms a low, spreading rosette of arching, spine-margined leaves that turn a striking reddish-purple to mottled bronze when grown hard in bright light, fading to duller green in shade. In the wild it colonizes limestone cliffs and dry rocky hillsides across northeastern Mexico and into southern Texas, tolerating extended drought, intense heat, and moderate freezes once established. It grows very slowly from seed, so the fastest way to build a planting is by dividing the basal offsets that mature clumps produce over time. Established colonies send up branched spikes of small white flowers, and the fibrous leaves were traditionally processed by indigenous communities in the region for cordage and coarse textiles.

planting.note: Plant small rooted clumps in spring into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun; this Argentine and Bolivian high-elevation bromeliad, formerly classified as Abromeitiella brevifolia, is grown exactly like a hardy succulent rather than a typical tank bromeliad.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun; Deuterocohnia brevifolia is made up of tiny, fleshy, toothed rosettes only about two inches across, but over many years the rosettes pack themselves together into a dense, mounded mat known as a 'polster' that can eventually spread several feet wide. Small greenish flowers appear tucked into the centers of individual rosettes from winter into early spring, adding little ornamental value compared with the striking cushion texture of the colony itself. Native to high, rocky slopes in Argentina and Bolivia, it is remarkably cold-hardy for a bromeliad relative, shrugging off hard freezes once established in soil that drains fast, and makes an excellent rock-garden or container specimen for growers who want a true xeriscape bromeliad that reads more like an alpine cushion plant. Division of a rooted section of the mat is the simplest way to start a new colony.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Plant of the Week

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into lean, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for lateral spread; this widespread Andean bromeliad forms large, dense clumps of narrow rosettes over time.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky, very well-drained soil in full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest, most intensely sunny climates. Deuterocohnia longipetala forms upright rosettes of narrow, gray-green, spine-edged leaves that clump and offset steadily into an expansive colony many feet across, one of the widest natural ranges of any Deuterocohnia, spanning dry rocky slopes and open scrub from Peru and Bolivia into northwestern Argentina. Established clumps send up tall flower spikes bearing yellow to orange blooms, often green-tipped, that appear in cooler months. It tolerates drought and poor, mineral soils with ease and takes light frost once mature, though it is less cold-hardy than the compact cushion-forming Deuterocohnia brevifolia, making it best suited to zone 9b and warmer or to large container culture elsewhere.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to light shade; this small Brazilian Atlantic Forest lithophyte grows on bare rock outcrops and needs sharp drainage rather than the moisture-holding tank typical of many bromeliads.

directions: Plant in a very well-drained, gritty succulent or bromeliad mix in full sun to light shade; Orthophytum saxicola is a diminutive, semi-succulent bromeliad endemic to rocky outcrops in the Atlantic Forest of Bahia, Brazil, forming a compact rosette of soft-spined, green to coppery-red leaves under six inches tall. It flowers from the rosette center with small white blooms, after which that rosette declines while offsets around the base continue the clump, so removing spent centers keeps plantings tidy. Because it grows naturally wedged into rock crevices with minimal soil, it is well suited to crevice gardens, trough plantings, and container culture with a lean, fast-draining mix, and it tolerates drought readily as long as it is not kept constantly wet. It is considerably more cold-tender than terrestrial genera like Dyckia or Hechtia and needs protection from frost, making it best treated as a warm-zone or container xeriscape accent rather than a garden plant in colder regions.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online
